activities.title: Be Resilient South Africa Project -  Citizen Sciences Component. The implemented activities forms part of the Be Resilient South Africa Project which aims to address climate risk and build adaptive capacity in SA's Biosphere Reserves.
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 1: Scientific Research and Innovation
activities.output_full: 1.10. Conducting and sharing of research on integrating citizen science in the hydrological discipline by the scient ific community and other stakeholders supported, to improve understanding of the water cycle enabling science based decision making
activities.description:
Citizen Sciences Component of the Be Resilient South Africa Project aims to strengthen data and knowledge management, research, capacity building with communities, and partnerships. 

The main activity under this component is the River Monitoring in 4 South African Biosphere Reserves
The activities include the following:
-Joint contextualization of the water quality and quantity problems in biosphere reserves involving youth, interested in Environmental Science 
-Co-creation of river monitoring programmes for the Eerste, Luvuvhu, Sand, Blyde and Marico catchments with the youth and biosphere reserves leads. 
-Training and capacity building for monitoring of water indicators including – miniSASS, pH, Dissolved Oxygen, E-coli, Electric Conductivity, Temperature, Turbidity, and stream flow. 
- Development, training, and use of a Smartphone Data Collection Application to capture citizen science data
- Development of understanding of catchment dynamics to enable a comprehensive mapping of causes of decline in water quality and availability. 
-Development of partnerships
activities.key_activity: 1.10.4. Continued Research and Development and capacity building work, including development of a citizen science toolbox, its promotion through training programmes and in cooperation with non-governmental organizations as catalysts.
activities.outcomes:
Citizen Science Data Collection and Visualization Platform: A mobile smartphone application specifically designed for citizen science data collection and visualization. This tool includes features for monitoring various water indicators such as miniSASS, pH, Dissolved Oxygen, E-coli, Electric Conductivity, Temperature, Turbidity, and stream flow.
Training, and Capacity Building Materials and Reports- Development and dissemination of training materials aimed at building the capacity of both the youth and biosphere reserve leads in monitoring water indicators. This includes the use of the training of various water indicators, smartphone applications, and Participatory Catchment Mapping Programmes
Partnerships - The establishment of partnerships among various stakeholders involved in the project, fostering collaboration and shared responsibility for effective river monitoring and environmental management.
Outcomes:
Strengthened Data and Knowledge Management through improved data collection, management, and knowledge dissemination related to water quality in the Biosphere Reserves.
Enhanced research and data collection - The project contributes to scientific research by providing valuable data on water indicators and catchment dynamics, helping to identify causes of decline in water quality. 
Capacity building through increased knowledge and skills among youth and biosphere reserve leads in environmental science and river monitoring, contributing to the development of local expertise.
 Active participation of communities, particularly youth interested in environmental science, in the joint contextualization and co-creation processes, fostering a sense of ownership and responsibility for local environmental issues.
Established partnerships through the development of partnerships among stakeholders, promoting collaboration and shared efforts for sustainable environmental management in the Biosphere Reserves
activities.institution: UNESCO Regional Office for Southern Africa
activities.partners: Kruger to Canyons Biosphere Reserve, Cape Winelands Biosphere Reserve, Groot Marico Biosphere Reserve, Vhembe Biosphere Reserve , Ground Truth, South African Environmental Observation Network,Quartex Technologies Stellenbosch Municipality

activities.title: The Horn of Africa Groundwater Access Facility (HoA-GaFa) Management Information System (MIS)
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 3: Bridging the data knowledge gap
activities.output_full: 3.3. Comparing and validating open access data on water quantity, quality and use and their sharing by the scientific community supported for sustainable water management.
activities.description: The Horn of Africa Groundwater Access Facility (HoA-GaFa) Management Information System (MIS) was hosted on IHP-WINS as a pilot use case. This integration aimed to assess the platform’s capability to manage, visualize, and analyze aquifer data for transboundary groundwater management. The MIS consolidates data such as well-logs, water quality reports, and geospatial information into a centralized system, enabling comprehensive data management and supporting sustainable groundwater provision for the region. The pilot highlighted the utility of IHP-WINS as a repository for standardized and validated aquifer data, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration among stakeholders.
activities.key_activity: 3.3.2. Facilitation and support for enhanced access to validated data, metadata and information, and coordinated access across the major water and related data bases, including the population and promotion of databases and platforms to make groundwater related data accessible to multiple stakeholders and improvement of the capabilities of the global MAR portal hosted by UNESCO-IGRAC.
activities.outcomes:
Capacity Building: Enhanced user skills in groundwater data management, standardization, and analysis through MIS integration with IHP-WINS.
Improved Data Availability: Centralized aquifer data improved accessibility and usability for stakeholders in the Horn of Africa.
Collaboration and Transparency: The use case fostered collaboration among researchers, policymakers, and NGOs, supporting interdisciplinary efforts in groundwater management.
Data-Driven Decision Making: The integration of MIS on IHP-WINS enabled evidence-based decision-making to address water stress and enhance groundwater sustainability.
Impact on Groundwater Monitoring: Strengthened ability to track and evaluate groundwater management projects using consolidated data visualizations and analytics.
activities.institution: UNESCO Regional Office for Eastern Africa
activities.partners: UNDP, UNICEF, IGAD
activities.stakeholder_group_type: Government Agencies (national water departments or ministries, environmental protection agencies, local government authorities responsible for water management)

activities.title: The Horn of Africa Groundwater Access Facility (HoA-GaFa) Training Workshop on IHP-WINS
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 3: Bridging the data knowledge gap
activities.output_full: 3.3. Comparing and validating open access data on water quantity, quality and use and their sharing by the scientific community supported for sustainable water management.
activities.description: The GAFA training workshop, held on November 27–28, 2024, served multiple objectives. Beyond equipping stakeholders from IGAD Member States with the skills to utilize the MIS hosted on IHP-WINS, the workshop emphasized the promotion of open-data sharing practices within the region. It provided a platform for user feedback on the functionalities and usability of IHP-WINS. Participants, including hydrogeologists, policymakers, and IT specialists, engaged in interactive sessions to understand system navigation, data entry, geospatial analysis, and advanced querying techniques. The workshop also facilitated discussions on improving the IHP-WINS platform and fostering regional collaboration in sustainable groundwater management.
activities.key_activity: 3.3.1. Enhancement of the capabilities and user friendliness of IHP-WINS, including the extension of IHP-WINS with new members, new data and new contributions from members.
activities.outcomes:
Knowledge Improvement: Over 20 participants enhanced their skills in using MIS tools for data management, standardization, and analysis.
Promotion of Open Data: Advocated for open-data sharing principles, increasing awareness and commitment to transparency among IGAD Member States.
User Feedback for Platform Improvement: Collected valuable insights from stakeholders to improve IHP-WINS functionalities and usability.
Capacity Strengthening: Improved ability of stakeholders to input, standardize, and retrieve groundwater and related geospatial data for decision-making.
Geospatial Analysis Proficiency: Participants developed skills in leveraging IHP-WINS geospatial tools for identifying groundwater trends and addressing water stress.
Enhanced Collaboration: Fostered interdisciplinary cooperation among IGAD governments, NGOs, and private stakeholders for transboundary groundwater management.
Data Standardization Practices: Established best practices for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of data integrated into IHP-WINS.
Sustainable Outcomes: Positioned IHP-WINS as a pivotal tool for integrated data management and open-data sharing, aligning with IHP-IX priorities of bridging the data-knowledge gap.

activities.partners: UNDP, UNICEF, IGAD

activities.title: CGIAR Research Initiative on Diversification in East and Southern Africa (Ukama Ustawi)
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 1: Scientific Research and Innovation
activities.output_full: 1.6. Scientific knowledge, methodologies and tools in addressing water related disasters, such as flood and drought elaborated and/or enhanced towards timely forecasting.
activities.description: This Initiative aims to support climate-resilient agriculture and livelihoods in 12 countries in East and Southern Africa by helping millions of smallholders intensify, diversify and reduce the risks in maize-based farming through improved extension services, small and medium enterprise development, supporting governance frameworks and increased investment with a gender and social inclusion lens.
activities.key_activity: 1.6.2. Science policy dialogue and capacity building on water management that considers wet and dry extremes (floods and drought), including symposia, workshops, and sessions in related events/fora.
activities.outcomes:
End-of-Initiative Outcomes: 
100,000 farmers, value chain actors and consumers (40% women and 40% youth) in maize-mixed systems are using climate-smart intensification & diversification practices with improved water and land management practices.
2 million farmers and other value chain actors (40% women and 40% youth) are accessing bundled digital agro-advisory and agricultural risk management (ARM) products and services that support their response to climate risks and manage land and water systems more sustainably for climate resilience.
Up to 60 agribusinesses (40% run by women and 40% run by youth) will have scaled climate smart solutions supporting diversification, intensification, and ARM of maize-mixed systems through at least US$7 million of new finance in debt, equity and grants that have been invested or are in the process of being invested.
US$200 million of investments enabled, and 4 strategies or policies developed or improved supporting collaborative governance and management of multifunctional landscapes.
US$ 25 million invested in scaling work in Eastern & Southern Africa for a Resilient Agri Food system

activities.title: DEVELOPMENT AND APPLICATION OF STANDARDIZED TOOLS TO SUPPORT ASSESSMENT OF THE SOCIO-ECONOMIC IMPACT OF WATER REALLOCATION THROUGH COMPULSORY LICENSING
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 4: Integrated Water Resources Management under conditions of Global Change
activities.output_full: 4.1. Conducting and sharing of research on inclusive and participatory approaches by the scientific community, to ensu re open, active, meaningful gender responsive engagement of youth, local and indigenous communities supported to enable all stakeholders to be part of the water management process.
activities.description:
This study, supported by the Water Research Commission and the Inkomati-Usuthu Catchment Management Agency and implemented by the International Water Management Institute, in collaboration with the University of the Witwatersrand and the Global Water Partnership, focuses on socio-economic impact assessments of water reallocation to contribute towards a more inclusive and democratic water resource management that overcomes historical injustices in South Africa.

The objectives of this study were to develop a set of simple, standardized and integrated tools and approaches for socio-economic assessments of water reallocation through compulsory licensing (CL) and to provide legal guidance on potential implications of severe prejudice to the economic viability of the undertaking as a result of compulsory licensing. A proposed framework was tested in the Inkomati-Usuthu Water Management Area (IUWMA) and refined.

The tools were informed by a literature review and interviews on the past three compulsory licensing processes (Tosca-Molopo, Jan Dissels, Mhlathuze), the current water reallocation scenarios in the Water Allocation Plans of the Inkomati-Usuthu Catchment Management Agency, and good international and national socio-economic valuation experiences and practices for inclusive socio-economic assessments of all water uses and users. The proposed tool is based on the monetary value generated (or contribution to GDP) per cubic metre (m3) of water both for those who gain and those who lose in reallocation. Expanding on this, the tool also analysed the related externalities and makes numerous implicit assumptions explicit for further assessment and quantification depending on data availability. The tool is integrated in national policy and legal frameworks by using the prioritization in the National Water Resource Strategy to make the socio-economic distinction between user groups and uses with higher priority (poverty eradication, livelihoods and racial and gender equity) and lower priority (large-scale commercial uses).
activities.key_activity: 4.1.1. Conducting and sharing scientific research in inclusive and participatory water management with gender emphasis and engagement of youth, local and indigenous communities, e.g. in selected demonstration sites (such as Ecohydrology demosites, CRIDA applications and UNESCO designated sites); studies and country level pilots including stock take on stakeholder participation in water management at all levels, and a country pilot showcasing modalities and benefits of engagement.
activities.outcomes:
Some of our key findings are, firstly, that in closed basins of the IUWMA any new water uptake by commercial large-scale industry or mining and any new water uptake by any priority 3 user (and priority 1, 2, or 4) should be provided by curtailment of priority 5 commercial agriculture.
Secondly, although we know that micro/small-scale agriculture and businesses by poor and marginalised households are likely to be many, we do not know how many users are involved or how much water they use in the IUWMA. Filling this data gap would be key to ensuring these “invisible users” are not excluded from the water allocation plan. The report estimates total hectarage of 30 000, which constitutes at least 15 000 farm households, taking 2 ha as a high average.

Thirdly, the data clearly show that irrigation by large-scale farming by 1207 farms is by far the main total water user, followed by forestry (2300 plantations), and that agricultural output per cubic metre is low compared to other sectors.
Fourthly, although mining and industry produce very high output per cubic metre of water, both sectors benefit only 442 enterprises. Moreover, they are likely to generate negative externalities through pollution, which need to be considered in the analysis.
Finally, once we measure the value of water in terms of survival, because without access to water survival could not be granted, then the value of water for domestic use is higher than any other sector.
Furthermore, this report offers legal guidance on the practical interpretation of 'severe prejudice to the economic viability of an undertaking' within the legal framework of the National Water Act, instilling confidence in the audience about its application. Throughout the project design, implementation and finalisation of reports, a Reference Group comprising officials and experts on the topic provided invaluable input.

activities.title: Indigenous Community-Based Strategies for Advancing Environmental Justice Through Water Quality Citizen Science
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 1: Scientific Research and Innovation
activities.output_full: 1.10. Conducting and sharing of research on integrating citizen science in the hydrological discipline by the scient ific community and other stakeholders supported, to improve understanding of the water cycle enabling science based decision making
activities.description: The Katari River Basin, a critical watershed for Lake Titicaca in the Andean region, faces severe water pollution from mining, urbanization, industrial activities, and agriculture. These pressures disproportionately affect Indigenous communities in the basin’s discharge area, exposing them to environmental hazards that compromise local water services, food security, and essential ecosystem services. This study investigates the potential of citizen science water quality monitoring as a tool for advancing environmental justice in Indigenous communities. Using a participatory, community-based approach, local stakeholders co-designed and implemented the project. Key activities included identifying community-specific water quality concerns, training citizen scientists in water quality monitoring techniques, and building capacity to link findings to national Indigenous rights and environmental governance frameworks. The study results revealed exceeded water quality standards, with elevated levels of nutrients, total dissolved solids, and electrical conductivity, underscoring the disproportionate environmental burden on Indigenous populations. These findings served as evidence for advocacy, fostering community engagement and raising awareness of systemic inequities. Importantly, the study revealed a lack of awareness among younger Indigenous generations, many of whom were born during the river’s prolonged state of hyper-eutrophication and thus had no reference to its prior ecological health. The project demonstrated the transformative role of citizen science in empowering communities, generating locally-relevant data, and catalyzing policy discussions. The study provides a replicable framework for understanding environmental justice challenges, emphasizing the dual role of citizen science as both a scientific tool and an advocacy platform for Indigenous and marginalized communities worldwide.
activities.key_activity: 1.10.2. Country and community level projects integrating indigenous knowledge in water and land management, through citizen and open science methodologies to build water resilience.
activities.outcomes:
Outcomes
Enhanced Community Empowerment
Indigenous communities in the Katari River Basin were empowered to take ownership of environmental monitoring and advocacy through active participation in citizen science.

Increased Awareness of Environmental Injustices
Local stakeholders and younger Indigenous generations gained a better understanding of water quality issues, systemic inequities, and their link to broader Indigenous rights and governance frameworks.

Evidence-Based Advocacy for Policy Change
Water quality data collected during the project was used as evidence to advocate for improved environmental governance and justice for the affected Indigenous communities.

Strengthened Environmental Justice Frameworks
The project contributed to integrating citizen science data into national Indigenous rights and environmental governance frameworks.

Replicable Methodology for Citizen Science
A participatory, community-based framework for addressing environmental justice challenges was developed, serving as a model for other marginalized communities worldwide.

Outputs
Locally-Relevant Water Quality Data
Data on water quality parameters, including elevated levels of nutrients, total dissolved solids, and electrical conductivity, indicating exceeded standards.

Capacity-Building Initiatives
Training sessions for community members on water quality monitoring techniques, fostering technical skills and local expertise.

Community-Designed Monitoring Plan
A collaboratively developed plan tailored to address specific water quality concerns of the Katari River Basin's Indigenous communities.

Advocacy Materials
Reports, presentations, and visual materials highlighting the project findings, serving as tools for raising awareness and driving policy discussions.

Engagement of Youth
Initiatives to involve younger Indigenous generations in understanding historical and current environmental challenges, bridging knowledge gaps.

Guidelines for Replication
Documentation of the participatory approach and methodology, providing a blueprint for similar citizen science initiatives in other regions.

activities.title: Citizen Science for Wetland Conservation: Unveiling Water Filtration Services in Kenya's Yala Swamp
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 1: Scientific Research and Innovation

activities.description: The Yala Swamp, a vital wetland ecosystem in Kenya, provides critical ecosystem services, including water filtration, biodiversity support, and livelihoods for surrounding communities. However, this wetland is increasingly threatened by environmental degradation and anthropogenic pressures. This study explores the role of citizen science in monitoring water quality and promoting conservation awareness. Collaborating with rural high schools and community members from Barkayango and Usenge, situated in the upper and lower reaches of the wetland, participatory water quality monitoring was conducted to assess spatial and temporal variations in key parameters such as turbidity, pH, electrical conductivity and nutrient levels. Preliminary results demonstrate the wetland's significant filtration capacity, with notable improvements in water quality downstream. The initiative facilitated capacity-building for local citizen scientists and catalyzed community discussions on the wetland’s ecological importance and the need for sustainable management. By integrating scientific inquiry with community engagement, this project emphasize the potential of wetlands as Nature-Based Solutions for regional water management. Furthermore, it highlights how citizen science can foster local stewardship, inform conservation policies, and support ecosystem resilience in the face of growing environmental challenges.

activities.title: Empowering Communities: Citizen Science for Water Quality in Cuba's Santa Clara Urban Sub Basin.
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 1: Scientific Research and Innovation
activities.output_full: 1.10. Conducting and sharing of research on integrating citizen science in the hydrological discipline by the scient ific community and other stakeholders supported, to improve understanding of the water cycle enabling science based decision making
activities.description:
The Sagua La Grande basin in Villa Clara, Cuba, faces significant environmental and economic challenges due to pollution and soil degradation. Spanning over 2,000 km2, this basin has over 79 identified sources of pollution, including electrochemical, mechanical, brewery, and preserves industries, which impact both inland and coastal waters. It also encompasses the city of Santa Clara, the provincial capital of Villa Clara, with a population of 250,000 residents.
The Arroyo Grande River and its tributaries, the Bélico and Cubanicay rivers, have been identified as the most polluted areas within the urban sub-basin of Santa Clara. To address these issues, a Citizen Science project has been proposed for this sub-basin. The main goal is to foster collaborative research and knowledge exchange in alignment with environmental education initiatives outlined in the Provincial Watershed Commission Report. The project aims to empower and involve community members living near the rivers, as well as university students, in addressing environmental pollution to raise awareness and achieve a reduction in contamination.
The methodology includes community participation in environmental education workshops, sampling of river water before and after it flows through the city, and monitoring of physicochemical variables to ensure reliable data that quantify the community's contribution to pollution. Parameters to be analyzed include pH, turbidity, electrical conductivity, salinity, temperature, nitrates, nitrites, hardness, and phosphates.
The expected outcomes of this project include identifying anthropogenic impacts to raise awareness and promote actions to improve water quality. The project is scheduled to begin in January 2025, with an initial implementation phase running through June and a second phase concluding in December, featuring monthly sampling campaigns. An evaluation of the first phase results will assess contamination thresholds.

activities.title: Guidelines for the assessment of groundwater quality
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 3: Bridging the data knowledge gap
activities.output_full: 3.4. Capacity of scientific community strengthened to develop, share and apply scientific tools for data processing (like data assimilation and visualization methods, quality assurance protocols to connect existing databases and outreach protocols).
activities.description:
The objective of the guidelines is to advocate and facilitate global-scale groundwater quality assessment, aligning with one of the key goals of the WWQA. The guidelines provide a structured methodology to make effective use of the available groundwater quality data towards global assessments. They have been developed to align with the SDG indicator6.3.2, which emphasizes three fundamental core parameters - pH, electrical conductivity and nitrate. Furthermore, these guidelines complement the SDG indicator 6.3.2 by introducing a methodology that incorporates additional general and site-specific water quality parameters relevant for the level-2 assessment. The main audiences of the guidelines include a wide range of international and national stakeholders and policy makers (e.g., United Nations, national water authorities),
by providing invaluable information for decision making, policy development, and collaborative efforts to protect and improve global and regional groundwater quality. These guidelines represent an initial step towards large-scale evaluations of groundwater quality. They are intended to encourage and promote the monitoring and assessment of groundwater quality and support the generation of useful information for decision-making based on monitoring data. As such, the developed guidelines complement, rather than replace, the comprehensive hydrogeochemical analysis conducted by local specialists.
activities.key_activity: 3.4.3. Development and sharing of data analysis methods including information fusion, data integration, assimilation, and visualization, e.g. through mobilization of UNESCO city networks like MAWAC.
activities.outcomes:
The groundwater quality guidelines through a series of case studies has brought to light several
pivotal insights:
• The Groundwater Quality Index (GQI) proves to be a valuable tool to facilitate groundwater quality assessment on regional and/or national scales. However, our case studies, particularly the one in Uganda, underscore the critical significance of data availability. Globally, groundwater data and information are often lacking or highly dispersed, which hiders the accurate evaluation of groundwater quality. We encourage countries to put more efforts on enhancing their monitoring networks to ensure a more comprehensive and representative assessment of groundwater quality.
• Besides the quantity of data, it’s also curial to maintain a strong focus on the quality of data to ensure the reliability of evaluation. This depends on several factors, including the quality of the monitoring network and the sources and objectives of data collection. Groundwater quality data often come from various sources applying different sampling protocols and analytical methods, making quality assurance and data harmonization a complex task. Efforts should be made to standardize data collection and quality assurance procedures.
• These guidelines serve as an initial step towards large-scale evaluations of groundwater quality. The purpose is to encourage and promote the monitoring and assessment of groundwater quality and facilitate the generation of useful information for decision-making. It's essential to note that these guidelines are designed to complement, rather than replace the comprehensive hydrogeological analysis conducted by local specialists. In this way the GQI also offers a way for national policymakers to assess the state of groundwater resources within and across their country (depending on data availability and quality of groundwater monitoring network) in order to prioritize actions where they are most needed.
• While the core focus of the guidelines is on human health, the underlying concept can also be further applied to assess groundwater quality for ecosystem protection, by adjusting parameters, weights and target values relevant for ecosystem functioning.
The methodology outlined in the proposed guidelines still has certain limitations that require further refinement.
• Limited parameters: The GQI calculation employs a limited number of parameters, potentially leading to the loss of information. It’s important to emphasize that the evaluation results exclusively rely on the parameters included in the GQI calculation and the available data, and additional quality concerns might exist due to pollutants that are not accounted for due to the limitation in parameters.
• Selection of site-specific parameters: The site-specific parameters are selected as the three “worst” parameters based on the predefined assessment units, such as river basins or aquifers. Future refinement may involve developing algorithms to select the site-specific parameters of interest at the monitoring well scale, to ensure that the calculated GQI represent the worst-case scenario at each sampling station.

activities.title: Groundwater chapter of the WMO State of the Global Water Resources report 2023
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 3: Bridging the data knowledge gap
activities.output_full: 3.1. Development and use of scientific research methods by the scientific community supported to correctly collect, analyze interpret and exchange data.
activities.description:
In 2024, based on the developed methodology in 2023, we have processed and analysed the data from 40 countries and prepared the groundwater chapter to contribute to the WMO report, which present the ranking of the groundwater level at each monitoring points, compared to the historical data series of 20 years. The report has been launched on October 7th, 2024.
The chapter evaluates groundwater levels in 2023 in comparison with historical records. It relies on in situ groundwater level monitoring data made available by the national (subnational, in some cases) institutions in charge of groundwater monitoring. In total, groundwater level monitoring data were collected for over 160 000 wells in 40 countries. Data were collected over the period covering the last 20 years, from 2004 to 2023. Where it was not possible to collect the data over this entire period, for instance in countries where groundwater monitoring is less than 20 years old, data covering the last 10 years were used instead. This is the case for Brazil, Bulgaria, Costa Rica and Israel. Groundwater level monitoring data were first filtered to guarantee a certain level of data consistency and completeness. After filtering, data could be analysed for some 35 459 of the wells. In total, the average groundwater level in 2023 was much below normal in 6 756 wells (19%), below normal in 4 087 wells (11%), normal in 14 030 wells (40%), above normal in 3 489 wells (10%) and much above normal in 7 097 wells (20%).
activities.key_activity: 3.1.3. Compilation and harmonization of knowledge products across sources and custodians of data and monitoring systems from collection, validation, analysis, assessment and reporting perspectives, in partnership with WMO; and engagement with the scientific community on the associated needs and the-state-of-the-art to stimulate research and enhance data services.
activities.outcomes:
The results are shown on a world map and on a selection of regional maps. The results show that the ranking is rarely uniform over a given area, because of the heterogeneous nature of aquifers and the importance of local variables influencing groundwater levels, such as a pumping well or the vicinity of a river. Nevertheless, regional patterns are observed, indicating that groundwater is also subject to regional influences.
The average groundwater level in 2023 was below normal or much below normal in a high proportion of wells over a large part of North America, in particular in the western and midwestern United States, and in central and northern Chile, western and southern Brazil, Southern Europe (Portugal, Spain, most of France), Central Europe (Hungary, Austria, Bavaria (Germany), the north of Poland), as well as in western and southern Australia. Conversely, the average groundwater level in 2023 was above normal or much above normal in a high proportion of wells in New England (United States), the Maritime provinces of Canada, along the Atlantic coast of north-eastern Brazil, Northern Europe (the British Isles and Scandinavia), Israel, Southern Africa, several parts of India, the Republic of Korea, eastern Australia, and the North Island of New Zealand.
Despite the significant number of countries covered in this evaluation, the data availability is such that large parts of the world are missing from this analysis, in particular in Africa and in Asia. This does not mean, however, that there are no data. There are several countries where groundwater level monitoring data have been collected for less than 10 years (such as the Gambia, Rwanda and Somalia). It will be possible to include these countries in the evaluation within a few years, which is a promising prospect. There are also challenges in accessing the latest data. Data from Croatia and Qatar could not be used because most of
the data from 2023 were not yet available for sharing.

activities.title: Low cost soil moisture sensors for drought applications at local scales
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 1: Scientific Research and Innovation
activities.output_full: 1.9. Development and sharing of new technologies using earth observation, Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things by the scientific community and service providers are communicated to and/or used for capacity strengthening of water stakeholders to increase their use in hydrological planning and assessment as well as monitoring and distribution networks.
activities.description:
The soil moisture sensors have been successfully installed in various countries in Africa and Central America (Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, Morocco, Rwanda, Tanzania and Cuba) reported in the first narrative report and the VUB continues to monitor the progress of data collection from the respective sites. As the sensors are not enabled with remote connection, the VUB provided a short training to field staff and researchers in the sites where the sensors are located. This included a training on how the sensors operate, how to use the Lolly software from the sensor manufacturer to configure the sensors to the appropriate time interval of data collection, and how to download the data to a local computer and visualizing it. A field demonstration was also given on how to properly install the sensors in the field and how to avoid damage to the sensor. For each site, an adapter was provided to accompany the sensor to enable data retrieval. A Python script was also prepared by the VUB to enable automated postprocessing of the raw soil moisture signal from the sensor to volumetric soil water content and availed to the researchers. Data from the sites is regularly retrieved and remitted to the VUB team where it is processed to its final format and stored. Since the sensors are not IoT enabled, data is manually retrieved and submitted to the VUB every 2-3 months. From then, the data is thoroughly validated to remove erroneous data. Alongside soil moisture, the dataset consists of three near-surface temperature measurements (12 cm ground surface (Temp: +12 cm), on the ground surface (Temp: 0 cm), and just below the surface (Temp: -6 cm). Measurements of soil moisture are collected at a depth of 15 cm below the ground using the Time Domain Transmittometry technique.
The TOMST loggers record soil moisture measurements as raw electric signals, which have to be converted to volumetric soil moisture content by a calibration approach. At the moment, a global calibration curve (independent of soil texture) is used as the data continues to be calibrated for different textures. The dataset includes the raw sensor readings, which can be calibrated using the TMS calibration guide https://tomst.com/web/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/TMS-calibration-handbook.pdf. To ensure interoperability between platforms the data is provided in an easy-to-interpret csv format consisting of the measurements, the coordinates of the data logger and the date since the data logger was deployed in the field. The soil moisture dataset has subsequently been uploaded to the UNESCO-IHP WINS.
activities.key_activity: 1.9.1. Facilitation of the development, and promotion, of tools and methodologies based on earth observations, Artificial Intelligence (AI) Machine Learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) for water resources assessment and monitoring and promote use of software applications such as rainwater harvesting, observation and as well as flood and drought monitoring.
activities.outcomes:
The outputs include:
-15 soil moisture sensors deployed in the case study areas
-Multi-year datasets of soil moisture and temperature at high temporal resolution
-Increased capacity of participating researchers to use these tools
-A comparative analysis of the performance of the sensors and remote sensing data
-A peer reviewed publication evaluating the applicability of the sensors to monitor drought at farm scale
-Python scripts to process the datasets

activities.title: Study of cryosphere components and associated hazardous exogenous processes
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 1: Scientific Research and Innovation
activities.output_full: 1.1. International scientific cooperation strengthened and fostered to address unsolved problems in hydrology, improving scientific understanding of hydrological cycles across river basins and aquifers.
activities.description: Study of cryosphere dynamics was organized and carried out using ground-based monitoring and remote sensing data
activities.key_activity: 1.1.1. activities.outcomes: Based on the high mountain research stations Tuiyksu Glacier (3450 m a.s.l.), Kishi Almaty river basin; Big Almaty Lake (2500 m) and Zhosaly kezen (3340 m) in Ulken Almaty river basin, year-round monitoring of the cryosphere (snow cover, glaciers, ground ice) was continued during the balance year (from October 2023 to September 2024). activities.description: In 2021 Diamonds on the Soles of our Feet (DSF) was a winner at the Falling Walls Engage, Berlin Science Week Summit for breaking down walls between science and society. The model has grown into a youth development programme working with schools as collaborative ecosystems.  What marks Diamonds as being different to many ‘science’ endeavours, is that it is  not just about data, data but it’s about empowering citizens and raising awareness about just how precious water is and the connection between humans and their natural environment.  We believe in the transformative potential of science through meaningful encounters with water. For us, Diamonds on the soles of our Feet is about transforming society and it’s about creating a more just world for people and the planet. It is about planetary health – a healthy planet and healthy people.
activities.key_activity: 1.5.3. Conducting and supporting scientific research to assess the interaction between humans, environment and water, in line with socio-hydrology within an urban rural setting and develop adaptive pathways, scenarios and strategies for water management.
activities.outcomes: A model for learning with the hear was developed. The model has now been anchored in a global project, DSF_Goes_Global with over 63 registrations in 15 different countries.  As such it is having a huge impact. In Kenya, for instance, the Mara Basin Conservation Forum is taking the model into 20 schools. There have been several important publications. The founder member is now mentoring other CS projects in Europe and is an active member of international citizen science task teams.

activities.notes: What has been remarkable is the way that DSF has grown as a learning from the heart model. It started off in the Limpopo but has now gone global. It has taken root for instance in Mexico, Peru, Uganda, Kenya - and beyond

activities.description:
1.1.	Workshops & Training Courses	
-Professional workshop of “Membrane Autopsy Techniques”
This specialized one-day workshop, convened by the UNESCO Chair on Water Reuse at the University of Tehran on September 21, 2023, provides an in-depth exploration of membrane autopsy techniques for the effective troubleshooting and diagnostic assessment of industrial water desalination systems. Under the tutelage of esteemed experts Dr. Mohammad Hossein Sarrafzadeh and Dr. Mojtaba Khani, the workshop caters to a diverse cohort of participants, encompassing industry practitioners, consultants, academics, researchers, and students with a vested interest in membrane-based water treatment technologies. The meticulously structured program is bifurcated into two integral phases: a theoretical component, elucidating fundamental principles of reverse osmosis (RO), intricate mechanisms of membrane fouling, and established autopsy methodologies; and a practical, hands-on component, affording participants invaluable experience in the examination of explanted membrane elements, the execution of precise sampling protocols, and the analytical evaluation of fouling phenomena.

The overarching objective of this intensive workshop is to empower participants with the requisite expertise to diagnose membrane performance anomalies, optimize the operational efficacy of desalination units, and implement effective mitigation strategies against fouling. The theoretical phase comprehensively addresses pivotal concepts, including the operational underpinnings of RO systems, the diverse typologies of membrane fouling, and standardized autopsy procedures. Concurrently, the practical phase furnishes participants with experiential learning opportunities in sampling methodologies, analytical techniques, and an introduction to a novel flat sheet membrane configuration.

activities.title: Strengthening sustainable water resources management of Subak Bengkel as best practices to support Subak system sustainability in Tabanan Regency in dealing with the challenges of climate change impacts.
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 4: Integrated Water Resources Management under conditions of Global Change
activities.output_full: 4.6. Undertaking and sharing assessment of ecosystem services and environmental flows in ecohydrology pilot sites by the scientific community supported, to improve integrated water resources management.
activities.description: The Subak Bengkel ecohydrology demonstration site offers an innovative model for sustainable water resource management, combining hydrological, ecological, and cultural strategies to address the challenges posed by climate change. This initiative aims to enhance the region by harmonizing water management practices with the local community’s cultural traditions and lifestyle. Key components include cultural preservation alongside capacity-building efforts that empower local communities to adopt climate-resilient agriculture. Comprehensive awareness-raising campaigns have been implemented to educate stakeholders about the multifaceted impacts of climate change, emphasizing its economic, social, health, and environmental ramifications, as well as highlighting effective, cost-efficient adaptation strategies. The project boasts significant potential for transferability and replicability, with outputs such as vulnerability assessments, integrated stormwater management approaches, GIS tools, and sustainable organic farming practices available for dissemination among interested parties. Additionally, the initiative seeks to enhance biodiversity across all its activities, aligning with the ethos of the Subak system, which embodies a unique blend of social, agricultural, and religious principles governed by customary law. This cooperative approach in managing water resources ensures that local needs for irrigation—critical for food production, aquaculture, animal husbandry, and tourism—are met sustainably. By fostering a culture of collaboration and shared responsibility, the Subak Bengkel site not only safeguards traditional practices but also establishes a robust framework for resilience in the face of ongoing climate challenges.
activities.key_activity: 4.6.2. Development/dissemination of case studies from current ecohydrology sites to improve the understanding of water ecosystem human interactions and highlight ecohydrology-NBS synergies.
activities.outcomes:
Following the Sustainable subak management objectives, the proposed Ecohydrology Demosite is:
•	Maintaining rainwater catchment areas in the upper of the river to keep the water quantity entering subak.
•	Strengthening waste and sediment trap in secondary or tertiary irrigation waterways to avoid water distraction into subak.
•	Enhancing household waste segregation management to minimize aquatic ecosystem disturbance.
•	Scaling up of bioremediation for water quality improvement in subak area.

Study of the Ecohydrology solutions effectiveness for the biodiversity is currently on progress. Meanwhile several potential activities should be implemented to strengthen biodiversity:
•	Changing in farm habits for all farmers through replacement of chemical fertilizers with organic fertilizers. 
•	Denaturalization of rivers green belt along the catchment area from upstream to downstream.
•	Cultivation of local’s owl species functioning as rats’ eradicator and food chain balancer in subak ecosystem.

The demosite is showing how to increase multiple ecosystem services, including:
•	Water quantity and quality management
•	Recreational areas as edu-ecotourism in farmland
•	Climate change mitigation in rural areas
•	Supporting biodiversity inside subak
•	Cultural and religious activities

activities.description:
Regional Training Centre for Water Resources and Irrigation (RCTWS) is a governmental organization under the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation (MWRI) in Egypt. It has been established in 1994 with the objective of enhancing the capacity building and human resources development in the water sector. Since 2002, it has been a Category II Water Centre, titled Regional Centre for Training and Water Studies, under the auspices of UNESCO. RCTWS focuses on key pillars which include learning and growth, financial sustainability, customer orientation, and quality assurance. The RCTWS helps in optimization of knowledge and technologies in water management processes.

The centre provides regional programs on integrated water management for African and Arab trainees, in addition to initiatives for civil society such as a course on utilizing water hyacinth for handicrafts. It ensures high-quality training by collaborating with professional trainers from various sectors. Continuous program development is one of the center's main goals that based on the training needs and the feedback from target groups, as well as pursuing accreditations for the training courses offered. The centre also has established cooperation protocols with academic institutions and local, regional, and international entities. RCTWS activities include curriculum development, quality assurance, and infrastructure improvement. Human resources development through training and coaching are of high priority for the centre.
activities.key_activity: 4.4.2. Promotion of source-to-sea and nexus approaches in water quality, quantity, ecosystems and biodiversity and resilience interlinkages; development of science-based guidance.
activities.outcomes:
The key outputs of RCTWS's activities include the development and implementation of regional training programs on integrated water management, civil society initiatives such as utilizing water hyacinth for handicrafts, and partnerships with academic and professional institutions. The center has also established cooperation protocols with local, regional, and international entities, and has developed capacity-building programs in line with the International Hydrological Programme (IHP-IX) and the African Water and Climate Adaptation (AWARe) initiative.

The outcomes of these activities include enhanced capacity building in the water sector, particularly in African and Arab countries, and the promotion of knowledge exchange and cooperation among professionals and stakeholders in the region. The center's activities have also contributed to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 6 on clean water and sanitation, and have supported adaptation to climate change in the water sector. Additionally, the center's training programs have equipped participants with the skills and knowledge needed to manage water resources effectively and efficiently, and have promoted the use of innovative technologies and approaches in water management. Overall, the outcomes of RCTWS's activities have been significant, and have made a positive impact on the water sector in the region.

They have managed to conduct awareness in the community.  It is an ongoing process that is conducted monthly (clean-up and water testing). Water testing is conducted with the assistance of DWS.

activities.description: This project addresses the rising concern over contaminants and pathogens in aquatic environments by developing adaptable and cost-effective smart sensor systems for water quality monitoring. Objectives include establishing a knowledge base, defining crucial sensor characteristics, evaluating promising technologies, and providing implementation recommendations. Evaluation of the Carbon Dioxide Evolution Measurement System (CEMS) showed low environmental contaminant concentrations had minimal impact on microbial metabolism. Near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy demonstrated precision in contaminant detection, but concerns arose regarding ecological relevance in diluted scenarios. The study advocates further research in NIR spectroscopy and highlights the potential of real-time, effect-based biosensors for the future of water quality monitoring.

activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 4: Integrated Water Resources Management under conditions of Global Change
activities.output_full: 4.3. Conducting and sharing of research on non conventional Water Resources (NCWRs) such as wastewater reuse, desalination, rainwater harvesting, and the Management of Aquifer Recharge (MAR) by the scientific community, in support of improving Water Cycle Management (WCM), strengthening capacities of local, regional, and national decision makers, and enhanced acceptance of public.
activities.description: The Sekhukhune District Municipality (SDM) is a mainly rural district  comprising four local municipalities and 764 villages. Water service delivery in the district is distributed, with a significant percentage of households having access to below RDP-level of service or no piped water at all, presenting an opportunity for the district to explore on-site domestic rainwater harvesting and stormwater harvesting systems. A simulation-optimization model for conjunctive use of surface and groundwater resources was developed and applied through a case study of existing reservoirs for one of the local municipalities. The model was used to idealize an appropriate allocation of surface and groundwater resources of the study area. Results show that the daily demand could be met without leading to over-abstraction of groundwater resources. However, failure to develop and implement water supply infrastructure maintenance plan and augmentation will result in a water crisis. For LID/Traditional developments, studies on cost-effectiveness of stormwater treatment trains need to be conducted.
activities.key_activity: 4.3.1. Research projects, including collaborative actions (private sector, NGOs, civil society) and compilation of the state of the art in NCRWs and circular economies to improve WCM and to enhance efficiency and effectiveness of public and private investments, also in urban and peri-urban settlements, and also in alignment with MAWAC (Megacities, Water & Climate).
activities.outcomes: A simulation-optimization approach for conjunctive use of surface and groundwater resources is developed and applied through a case study of existing reservoirs for Elias Motsoaledi Local Municipality

activities.title: Development of datasets for multi-scale water resource assessments towards a water secure South Africa
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 4: Integrated Water Resources Management under conditions of Global Change
activities.output_full: 4.1. Conducting and sharing of research on inclusive and participatory approaches by the scientific community, to ensu re open, active, meaningful gender responsive engagement of youth, local and indigenous communities supported to enable all stakeholders to be part of the water management process.
activities.description:
Assessments of water resources and crop production across South Africa are frequently based on estimates produced using deterministic hydrological and crop simulation models, due to either insufficient measured data or the need to assess the impacts of climate change and land use change. Such large-scale model configurations are in themselves data intensive and dependent on good quality data inputs. In conjunction with simulation models, the Quinary Catchments Database (QnCDB) and its predecessor, the Quaternary Catchments Database (QCDB), have provided a valuable assessment tool over the past two decades. As a first step towards updating and extending the QnCDB, this project aimed to:
1) develop a collection of national scale datasets for application in water resource-related modelling assessments and flood estimation, and 
2) develop, or utilise an existing online data portal to store and provide access to these datasets.
activities.key_activity: 4.1.1. Conducting and sharing scientific research in inclusive and participatory water management with gender emphasis and engagement of youth, local and indigenous communities, e.g. in selected demonstration sites (such as Ecohydrology demosites, CRIDA applications and UNESCO designated sites); studies and country level pilots including stock take on stakeholder participation in water management at all levels, and a country pilot showcasing modalities and benefits of engagement.
activities.outcomes:
The following datasets were developed:
1) A set of sub-Quaternary hydrological watershed catchment boundaries (called Quinary Catchments or QnCs) that are nested within the DWS 2018 Quaternary Catchment (QC) boundaries.
2) An updated (i.e. version 2) set of sub-Quaternary altitude zones (called Altitude Zones or AZs) that are also nested within the DWS 2018 QC boundaries.
3) A vector dataset of river reaches with associated attributes, that is compatible with the QnC boundaries, providing a QnC level river flow network that facilitates the configuration of hydrological models.
4) A set of climatic (e.g. rainfall and temperature) and topographic characteristics (e.g. mean altitude and slope) for each QnC and AZ.
5) For each QnC and AZ within South Africa, datasets of hydrological soil characteristics based on terrain unit level soils data.

activities.key_activity: 1.6.1. Research and knowledge generation on the scientific advances in addressing and timely forecasting of water related disasters, such as (flash) floods, (flash) droughts and rainfall induced landslides; and on additional impact of synchronous and/or cascading water related hazards, in partnership with EGU, AGU, IAHS ISEH and ICL - International Consortium on Landslides and IPL - International Programme on Landslides including good practices and lessons learned.

activities.stakeholder_group_type: Government Agencies (national water departments or ministries, environmental protection agencies, local government authorities responsible for water management)
activities.notes:
This activity is a joint UK-Ghana contribution to IHP-IX, with both the UK and Ghana supporting the implementation of the activity.

As part of the activity, after the one-day workshop, researchers from UKCEH visited various operational and research institutions of Ghana for more in-depth discussions.

A more detailed summary on the outputs and outcomes:  The workshop identified key challenges in hydrological and drought management for Ghana, particularly limited observational and forecasting datasets. Ghana expertise on such topics along with UKCEH experience with innovative methods on such topics along with can help bridge these gaps. One of the main outcomes can be to integrate global model forecasts with local predictions for high-impact hydrological stations, into one comprehensive forecasting system to enhance regional prediction capabilities.

Understanding drought impacts emerged as a critical focus area. Future work will explore region-specific impact datasets, including crop yields, livestock mortality, and malaria cases, as proxies for drought severity. Additionally, UKCEH’s high-resolution, open-access global drought indicator datasets will be utilized. Planned collaboration with WRI will facilitate their integration into machine-learning models for impact-based drought forecasting. Immediate steps include engaging visiting scientists from Ghana to co-develop these models with UKCEH experts. 

Capacity building was another priority, with plans to provide training in hydrological modelling and forecasting techniques. A long-term goal is to establish UKCEH West Africa Office as a hub for future collaborations, strengthening resilience to climate extremes through data sharing, research partnerships, and technical exchanges.

Through GWEN, the founding partners will contribute to the following objective : “Develop and deliver on a common global agenda to accelerate capacity development for the water sector in low- and middle-income countries”. As a means to this end, GWEN is designed as a coordination mechanism consisting of the founding partners, with a clear governance structure, operating in collaboration with existing networks, institutions and
organizations. By means of coordination through GWEN as well as implementing activities that contribute to this agenda, founding partners strive to address SDG6 related capacity development challenges.
More specifically, main objectives of GWEN as a coordination mechanism are to:
1. Deliver capacity development service in support of national governments and other key water organizations to identify and address education and capacity gaps through demand driven activities.
2. Develop co-curated capacity development products, services, and instruments to allow GWEN members to
jointly deliver state of the art capacity development services.

improve sharing of lessons learned, trends and insights related to capacity development and water education.

This publication follows a thorough mapping exercise of existing actors, activities, initiatives, tools and methodologies that contribute to each of the identified components of Open Hydrology. The Open Hydrology framework advocates for the accessibility of hydrological research to a broad spectrum of researchers, practitioners, and policymakers. Free and equal access to hydrological knowledge, technology, and tools is indispensable for FAIR advancement and innovation in addressing the current intricate water challenges.

The specific aim of the survey was to identify the factors that hinder and promote open science in hydrology research and education. The survey collected 61 responses and highlighted the importance of open data collection, analysis, and publishing in hydrology research. All results were integrated in the publication. Further, the publication also showcases specific case studies that stand as an example of Open Hydrology applications.

This online Open Learning course ‘Introduction to HEC-HMS modeling’ was developed in collaboration with the US Army Corps of Engineers and introduces the Hydrologic Modeling System, HEC-HMS, focusing both on using the program and performing watershed studies. The course topics include:
•	GIS tools to delineate subbasins and streams, GIS tools to extract physical characteristics and estimate model parameters.
•	Basin average rainfall estimation, infiltration determination, unit hydrographs, streamflow routing.
•	Methods for modeling runoff throughout a watershed composed of multiple subbasins and river reaches. Steps to calibrate the HMS model is also included. Live sessions provide hands-on reinforcement for topics covered in the lectures and will demonstrate the application of the HEC-HMS software.

These live sessions allowed to review the released modules with possibility for Q&A with the instructors and to provide demonstrations of advanced software features. Over 580 users expressed interest in the course. Of the users that indicated their gender (24%), 20% were female, and 80% male. 85 participants managed to complete the course and received the certificate.

activities.key_activity: 5.2.4. Capacity development of stakeholders in implementing sound and adaptive, context specific and location-based water governance in local, national and transboundary water resources with focus on climate change and water related disasters.
activities.outcomes:
By mapping vulnerable areas that are affected by climate change, such as Small Island Developing States (SIDS), we can assist governments and aid organizations like the Red Cross in providing more effective emergency assistance. Identifying the locations of buildings, roads, water sources, health facilities, and other essential infrastructure through mapping enhances the ability to monitor situations and improves the delivery of vital services.
In this context, participants focused on mapping buildings in the Monte Cristi West zone of the Dominican Republic. This effort aimed to generate critical data that can be used for disaster risk reduction planning and improving emergency response strategies. The use of the Hot Task Manager (https://tasks.hotosm.org/) platform with the support of the collective Missing Maps facilitated this process, allowing participants to collaborate effectively and contribute to the enhancement of the world map. More than 5500 buildings have now been mapped in the target area of the Dominican Republic.

activities.title: Mapping of Water-related Disaster Emergency Response
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 5: Water Governance based on Science Mitigation, Adaptation and Resilience
activities.output_full: 5.1. Awareness raising of decision makers at all levels on the importance of science based water governance by the UNESCO Water Family supported, to enhance the overall resi lience of communities to effects of global change.
activities.description:
Natural hazards such as floods, hurricanes, and earthquakes pose serious threats, which are increasingly exacerbated under the influence of climate change. The growing frequency and intensity of water-related hazards—from natural hazards to human-induced emergencies—underscore the urgent need for comprehensive disaster response strategies. In the wake of such catastrophes, a complex landscape of heightened human suffering, financial losses, and significant impacts on biodiversity emerges.
Addressing post-disaster challenges necessitates the deployment of specialized technologies guided by scientific insights. There is a significant opportunity to deliver tailored responses to the evolving needs of disaster-affected communities. As this potential remains largely untapped, a mapping exercise is being developed to explore the feasibility of establishing a rapid response mechanism for water-related disasters, including floods, droughts, landslides and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods.
activities.key_activity: 5.1.4. Engagement with public decision-makers in development planning, pandemic and disaster response, and climate change adaptation/mitigation to provide science-based water input.
activities.outcomes:
This mapping exercise involves a comprehensive review of existing emergency response mechanisms for water-related disasters, particularly those supported by the World Bank Group, European Union, and United Nations. The exercise will also identify potential rapid actions that can be implemented to address water-related disasters in the short term (0-3 months) and medium term (3-6 months). 
Additionally, an online survey will assess the current emergency response capacity to water-related disasters within the IHP Water Family. This assessment will enable us to align available capacities with potential rapid actions, thereby enhancing emergency response efforts for water-related disasters.

activities.title: Training on Open Hardware & Open Software Solutions for Sustainable Development in South-Africa
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 1: Scientific Research and Innovation
activities.output_full: 1.10. Conducting and sharing of research on integrating citizen science in the hydrological discipline by the scient ific community and other stakeholders supported, to improve understanding of the water cycle enabling science based decision making
activities.description:
The Workshop on Open Hardware & Open Software Solutions for Sustainable Development took place from 13-17 May 2024 in Cape Town, South Africa. This training brought together around 50 leading experts, scientists, and practitioners from across the African region from various institutes to delve into the latest advancements in Open Hardware and Open Software.

Open Hardware and Open Software solutions can play a crucial role for sustainable development. By enabling transparency and collaboration, these solutions can lead to the creation of sustainable technologies that are easily adaptable to local contexts. This workshop offered two concurrent training sessions: one focused on Open Hardware and the other on Open Software, both featuring hands-on exercises, lectures, demonstrations, and field applications.
activities.key_activity: 1.10.4. Continued Research and Development and capacity building work, including development of a citizen science toolbox, its promotion through training programmes and in cooperation with non-governmental organizations as catalysts.
activities.outcomes:
The workshop aimed to train participants on new concepts of Open Hardware, Open Software, Internet-of-Things, Citizen Science and Artificial Intelligence, with a particular focus on their applications in environmental and water resources management. This initiative aligns with the UNESCO Recommendation on Open Science, promoting open access, transparency, and collaboration to foster sustainability and equity. 

A field visit allowed participants to explore the application of the concepts in real-world settings through several engaging activities. The participants examined the use of IoT sensors in the Eerste Rivier, highlighting the potential of real-time monitoring to support flood warnings. In the Cape Winelands Biosphere Reserve, a demonstration showcased Citizen Science applications using different instruments along with the smartphone application developed by Quartex as part of the Citizen Science toolbox. Additionally, the challenges and solutions associated with a field installation pilot in the Kruger to Canyons Biosphere Reserve were addressed, providing further insights into the practical implementation of these technologies.

The workshop also provided a platform for networking and knowledge exchange. Participants had the opportunity to share their experiences, discuss challenges, and explore potential collaborations and specific follow-up actions to the course in four working groups. Each group formulated detailed work plans to continue efforts in Africa across key areas: Open Hardware, Open Software, Citizen Science, and Artificial Intelligence. These strategic plans are expected to drive further progress and ensure the sustained application of the knowledge and skills gained during the workshop.

activities.description: The capacity building workshop sought to enable the National IHP Committee mobilize stakeholders towards priorities for Kenya during the implementation of the IHPIX Strategic Plan. The regional workshop established a network of personnel (public and private) who can contribute to the IHP IX objectives and deliverables; while contributing to the science-policy interphase as ascribed in UNESCO’s water strategy for 2022-2029, titled “Science for a Water Secure World in a Changing Environment” (IHP-IX).

activities.outcomes:
- Establishment of Kenya's priority areas during the implementation of the IHPIX Strategic Plan.
- Stakeholders mapping within the water sector, their roles, review water related challenges and priorities.
- Familiarisation with current trends in water sector and issues, opportunities that exist including funding mechanisms, technologies and networks.
- Network of personnel (public and private) who can contribute to the IHP IX objectives and deliverables.
- Enhanced science-policy interphase as ascribed in UNESCO’s water strategy for 2022-2029.

activities.title: Recherche Scientifique  et Innovation
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 1: Scientific Research and Innovation
activities.output_full: 1.6. Scientific knowledge, methodologies and tools in addressing water related disasters, such as flood and drought elaborated and/or enhanced towards timely forecasting.
activities.description:
L’activité du Comité National PHI Sénégal porte sur l’amélioration des connaissances et de la gestion des ressources en eau à travers la recherche scientifique et l’innovation. Elle s’articule autour de plusieurs axes :

1. Télémesure et hydrologie spatiale : Mise en place d’un réseau de télétransmission pour suivre les données hydrométéorologiques, incluant 31 stations hydrométriques et 9 stations météorologiques. Acquisition de données hydrologiques satellitaires pour surveiller les bassins du fleuve Sénégal et de la Gambie.

2. Technologies avancées : Installation de stations hydrométriques automatiques (PS-Light2), utilisation de drones pour des levées bathymétriques et hydrologiques, et production de bulletins hydrologiques pour des alertes en temps quasi réel.

3. Recherche et formation : Organisation de la conférence FRIEND-WATER Global Dakar 2023 sur les défis hydrologiques, avec des formations en écohydrologie, hydrométrie et systèmes d’alerte précoce.

4. Gouvernance et coopération : Développement d’un cadre de gestion du Bassin Aquifère Sénégalo-Mauritanien (BASM), mise en place d’un groupe de travail et d’un secrétariat permanent.

5. Planification et gestion de l’eau : Élaboration de documents stratégiques (SDAGE, PDDI), modélisation des ressources en eau et étude des impacts du changement climatique sur les fleuves.

L’objectif global est de renforcer la connaissance et la gouvernance des ressources en eau pour une gestion durable face aux défis climatiques.
activities.key_activity: 1.6.1. Research and knowledge generation on the scientific advances in addressing and timely forecasting of water related disasters, such as (flash) floods, (flash) droughts and rainfall induced landslides; and on additional impact of synchronous and/or cascading water related hazards, in partnership with EGU, AGU, IAHS ISEH and ICL - International Consortium on Landslides and IPL - International Programme on Landslides including good practices and lessons learned.
activities.outcomes:
La Direction de la Gestion et de la Planification des Ressources en Eau (DGPRE) a mis en œuvre le Programme Hydrologique Intergouvernemental (PHI) afin de renforcer la gestion durable des ressources en eau. Parmi ses principaux produits, on retrouve : 
- Des cartes hydrologiques et hydrographiques, qui permettent de mieux comprendre la répartition des ressources en eau.
- Des bases de données hydrologiques, intégrant des informations sur les niveaux des nappes et les débits des cours d’eau.
- Une meilleure surveillance des ressources en eau grâce à des stations hydrométriques modernisées et des modèles de gestion des bassins versants permettant une exploitation plus rationnelle. 
- Des rapports et études hydrologiques qui soutiennent la planification et l’adaptation aux changements climatiques.
- Le renforcement des capacités à travers des formations pour les acteurs locaux et la sensibilisation des populations sur l’importance d’une gestion durable des ressources en eau. 

Ces efforts ont contribué à une prise de décision plus efficace et à une gouvernance améliorée des ressources hydriques au niveau national.

activities.title: Open Science Platform 2.0
activities.priority_area_full: Priority Area 1: Scientific Research and Innovation
activities.output_full: 1.4. Conducting scientific research on the exploration of new business models, the role of water utilities, broadening engagement and partnerships, and infrastructure by the scientific community supported to accelerate the circular economy tr ansition of the water sector
activities.description: The Ministry of Science, Technological Development, and Innovation of the Republic of Serbia elected members for the Team for Open Science in Serbia (TONuS) in February 2024. Dr. Brankica Majkić-Dursun, director of the WSDAC Center, was elected as a member. The TONuS team has decided to actively work on improving the Open Science Platform in the Republic of Serbia, with the goal of adopting an innovative version by December 2024. Throughout 2024, the TONuS team held several national-level meetings. In December 2024, the new Platform for Open Science was adopted. The platform represents an important step towards enhancing scientific cooperation, increasing the availability of scientific results in our country, and laying the foundation for expanding the principles of open science in Serbia.
activities.key_activity: 1.4.3. Intersectoral dialogue among public, private and civil water stakeholders for promoting the circular economy transition of the water sector an d of other industry sectors and expansion of good practices
activities.outcomes: Platform 2.0 implies the realization of five goals: (1) open access to scientific literature; (2) availability of research data; (3) open and transparent access to research infrastructures; (4) transparency of scientific communication and methodology, including the availability of software source code, project documentation of research hardware and other digital objects used in the analysis of research data, which enable the sustainability, transparency and reproducibility of scientific results, as well as (5) the development of digital infrastructure and competencies that enable the achievement of the stated goals. The realization of these goals should contribute to greater visibility of scientific results, better utilization of budget funds invested in research, greater connection between science, economy and society, greater scientific integrity, building trust in science, as well as the development of new research and innovations.
activities.institution: Ministry of Science, Technological Development and Innovation Republic of Serbia
activities.partners: WSDAC Centre, Faculties, Universities, Research Institutes from Serbia
activities.knowledge_product_type_other: National improved Platform for Open Science 2.0
activities.notes: We are unsure how to appropriately present the activity establishing the Platfrom for Open Science 2.0 in Serbia, considering that the adopted Open Science Platform 2.0 covers a wide range of priority activities, not only in the field of water resources but also in other areas. Since WSDAC had a nominated delegate who contributed to the establishment of Platform 2.0, we have presented it as an activity of our center for 2024. The National Open Science Platform is, among other things, based on the UNESCO Recommendation on Open Science, 2021 document. The final document can be accessed via this link: http://www.open.ac.rs/images/doc/TONuS-Platforma_2.0-Final.pdf, and the website of the TONuS Open Science team is available here: http://www.open.ac.rs/index.php. If you believe that this activity is not suitable for the IHP-9 phase, please remove the result from the database.
